stem: A 62-year-old stable on a dihydropyridine starts drinking grapefruit juice daily and develops flushing and ankle edema. A second patient's CCB stops working after rifampin. Which statement explains both?

options.A: Grapefruit lowers dihydropyridine levels; rifampin raises CCB levels
options.B: Grapefruit raises dihydropyridine levels; rifampin lowers CCB levels
options.C: Both raise CCB levels by blocking renal clearance
options.D: Neither changes levels; both act on digoxin instead
options.E: Both lower CCB levels by enzyme induction

why: Rifampin and carbamazepine lower CCB levels; grapefruit juice raises dihydropyridine levels.

whys.C: Rifampin lowers levels.
whys.D: Verapamil and diltiazem are what raise digoxin.
whys.E: Grapefruit raises levels.

takeaway: Grapefruit up, rifampin down.
discriminator: Inhibition and induction of the same drugs.

stem: An 80-year-old woman started chlorthalidone 3 weeks ago. Her daughter reports new confusion and unsteadiness. Which lab abnormality is the most likely cause?

options.A: Hyponatremia, which can be significant in older adults
options.B: Hypermagnesemia, because thiazides block its excretion
options.C: Hypocalcemia, because thiazides waste calcium in urine
options.D: Hyperkalemia, because thiazides spare potassium
options.E: Hypoglycemia, because thiazides raise insulin release

why: Thiazide adverse effects: hyponatremia (can be significant, especially in older adults), hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia and hypercalcemia. Monitor sodium, potassium, calcium and glucose.

whys.B: This is not a taught thiazide effect.
whys.C: Thiazides lower urinary calcium and can raise serum calcium.
whys.D: Thiazides cause hypokalemia.
whys.E: They cause hyperglycemia.

takeaway: Older adult + new thiazide + confusion = check sodium.
discriminator: Thiazide lows: Na, K. Thiazide highs: glucose, uric acid, Ca.

stem: A 64-year-old with stable angina took sildenafil last evening. He now has chest pain and reaches for his sublingual nitroglycerin. Why is this dangerous?

options.A: Both constrict the afferent arteriole: kidney injury
options.B: Both cause reflex bradycardia and AV block
options.C: Both raise cGMP: life-threatening hypotension
options.D: Sildenafil causes nitrate tolerance within hours
options.E: Sildenafil blocks nitrate absorption under the tongue

why: Nitrates donate NO and raise cGMP; PDE5 inhibitors block cGMP breakdown. Together they cause life-threatening hypotension.

whys.B: That is the verapamil or diltiazem with beta-blocker risk.
whys.D: Tolerance comes from continuous nitrate exposure.
whys.E: The interaction is additive vasodilation.

takeaway: Nitrate + PDE5 inhibitor: never.
discriminator: Make more cGMP + stop its breakdown.

stem: A 72-year-old with heart failure and CKD takes lisinopril. Spironolactone is added. Which monitoring plan matches the lecture?

options.A: Magnesium and hearing tests within 1 month
options.B: Serum osmolality and electrolytes each day
options.C: Potassium and creatinine within 1 week
options.D: Potassium and creatinine at the next annual visit
options.E: Sodium and glucose within 1 week

why: Spironolactone: monitor potassium and creatinine within 1 week. Hyperkalemia risk rises sharply with an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or in CKD.

whys.B: That is mannitol monitoring.
whys.D: Hyperkalemia here can be life-threatening and early.
whys.E: Those are the thiazide labs.

takeaway: Spironolactone + ACE inhibitor + CKD: potassium in a week.
discriminator: Each diuretic class has its own lab set.

stem: A 29-year-old at 14 weeks of pregnancy needs an antihypertensive. Among the drugs on the lecture's 'other antihypertensives' slide, which is named for use in pregnancy?

options.A: Isosorbide mononitrate
options.B: Clonidine
options.C: Spironolactone
options.D: Methyldopa
options.E: Hydralazine alone

why: Methyldopa is the central alpha2 agonist used in pregnancy.

whys.B: Its taught point is rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal.
whys.C: It is the add-on for resistant hypertension.
whys.E: Its taught point is pairing with a beta-blocker and diuretic.

takeaway: Pregnancy: methyldopa.
discriminator: Same receptor as clonidine, different use.

stem: A 61-year-old on lisinopril for 3 months has a dry, nagging cough with clear lungs. A second patient on lisinopril arrives with lip and tongue swelling. Which pair of actions is correct?

options.A: Cough: switch to amlodipine. Swelling: switch to verapamil
options.B: Cough: switch to an ARB. Swelling: stop the drug now
options.C: Cough: add an antihistamine. Swelling: lower the dose
options.D: Cough: continue unchanged. Swelling: add a diuretic
options.E: Cough: stop all RAAS blockade. Swelling: switch to an ARB

why: ACE inhibitors let bradykinin accumulate: dry cough (the most common reason to switch to an ARB) and, rarely, angioedema, which requires stopping the drug.

whys.A: An ARB keeps RAAS blockade without the bradykinin effect.
whys.C: The cough is bradykinin-mediated, not allergic.
whys.D: Angioedema can be life-threatening: stop the drug.
whys.E: Cough alone is the commonest reason to switch, not abandon.

takeaway: Cough → ARB. Angioedema → stop.
discriminator: Both are bradykinin; only one is dangerous.

stem: A 59-year-old receiving gentamicin for sepsis develops pulmonary edema. A colleague plans IV furosemide 80 mg as a 1-minute push. Which concern is most specific to this plan?

options.A: Lithium-like toxicity; loops raise aminoglycoside levels
options.B: Additive ototoxicity; give IV furosemide no faster than 4 mg/min
options.C: Hypercalcemia; loops reduce urinary calcium excretion
options.D: Metabolic acidosis; loops waste bicarbonate in the urine
options.E: Hyperkalemia; check potassium before any loop diuretic

why: Loop ototoxicity occurs with rapid IV administration or high doses and is additive with aminoglycosides. IV furosemide is given slowly, no faster than 4 mg/min.

whys.A: Lithium levels rise with thiazides; this is a different issue.
whys.C: Loops raise urinary calcium; thiazides lower it.
whys.D: Loops cause metabolic alkalosis.
whys.E: Loops lower potassium.

takeaway: Loop + aminoglycoside, or a fast push: ears at risk.
discriminator: Rate and co-drug, not the diuretic alone.

stem: A 74-year-old takes losartan and furosemide. After a week of over-the-counter ibuprofen for knee pain, creatinine has doubled. Which explanation is most complete?

options.A: Ibuprofen alone is directly toxic to the renal tubules
options.B: Losartan caused bradykinin build-up in the glomerulus
options.C: Furosemide caused hyperkalemia that injured the kidney
options.D: Efferent constriction from ibuprofen raised filtration
options.E: Afferent constriction, efferent dilation and volume loss together

why: NSAID (afferent constriction) + ACE inhibitor or ARB (efferent dilation) + diuretic (volume depletion): filtration pressure collapses. Common, often missed and preventable; ask about OTC NSAIDs.

whys.A: The lecture's point is the three combined hemodynamic hits.
whys.B: ARBs do not act through bradykinin.
whys.C: Loops lower potassium.
whys.D: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole and filtration falls.

takeaway: ACEi/ARB + diuretic + NSAID = AKI.
discriminator: Each drug alone is tolerated; the three together are not.

stem: A patient taking oral furosemide 80 mg is switched to bumetanide. Which statement about relative potency matches the lecture?

options.A: The two are equal, mg for mg
options.B: Potency cannot be compared between loop diuretics
options.C: Bumetanide is about 4 times as potent, mg for mg
options.D: Bumetanide is about 40 times as potent, mg for mg
options.E: Furosemide is about 40 times as potent, mg for mg

why: Bumetanide is about 40× furosemide mg for mg.

whys.A: Bumetanide is far more potent per mg.
whys.B: A conversion is taught.
whys.C: The taught ratio is about 40.
whys.E: The ratio runs the other way.

takeaway: Bumetanide 1 mg ≈ furosemide 40 mg.
discriminator: Same class and site; very different mg dose.

stem: A 44-year-old stable on lithium for bipolar disorder starts hydrochlorothiazide. Two weeks later he has a coarse tremor, vomiting and ataxia. What happened?

options.A: Lithium raised the thiazide level and caused hyponatremia
options.B: An NSAID effect: the thiazide blunted lithium clearance
options.C: The thiazide raised his lithium level
options.D: The thiazide lowered his lithium level
options.E: The pair caused hyperkalemia through aldosterone blockade

why: Lithium levels rise with thiazides. New neurologic and GI symptoms after the diuretic is added are lithium toxicity.

whys.A: The taught direction is thiazide raising lithium.
whys.B: NSAIDs blunt diuretics; no NSAID is involved here.
whys.D: Lower levels would cause relapse, not toxicity.
whys.E: Neither drug blocks aldosterone.

takeaway: Thiazide + lithium = lithium toxicity.
discriminator: Which drug's level moved: lithium's.

stem: A 36-year-old takes acetazolamide for a high-altitude trek. Labs afterward show low bicarbonate and low potassium, and she passes a kidney stone. How should this be read?

options.A: These are loop effects; she was given the wrong drug
options.B: The acidosis is expected; potassium loss and stones are not
options.C: None is expected; acetazolamide causes alkalosis
options.D: All three are predictable effects of acetazolamide
options.E: The stone is expected; acidosis means a second illness

why: Acetazolamide (glaucoma, altitude sickness, alkalosis) causes a mild metabolic acidosis as a predictable effect, plus potassium loss; watch for kidney stones.

whys.B: All three are taught effects.
whys.C: It is used for alkalosis and causes acidosis.
whys.E: Mild metabolic acidosis is predictable.

takeaway: Acetazolamide: acidosis, low potassium, stones.
discriminator: The only diuretic here that causes acidosis.

stem: A 70-year-old wears a nitroglycerin patch 24 hours a day. After a month his angina has returned at the same exertion. Adherence is perfect. Which change is best?

options.A: Add sildenafil to boost the nitrate's cGMP signal
options.B: Add verapamil to his metoprolol for more rate control
options.C: Stop the patch abruptly because of rebound hypertension
options.D: Double the patch strength and keep 24-hour wear
options.E: Schedule a nitrate-free interval, typically overnight

why: Tolerance develops with continuous nitrate exposure. A nitrate-free interval, typically overnight, is required to maintain efficacy with long-acting formulations.

whys.B: That pair risks bradycardia and AV block.
whys.C: Rebound hypertension is the clonidine issue.
whys.D: More continuous exposure deepens tolerance.

takeaway: Long-acting nitrate: build in a nitrate-free interval.
discriminator: Lost effect from tolerance, not from under-dosing.

stem: A 67-year-old with heart failure takes digoxin and has had furosemide increased twice this month. She now has nausea, visual changes and new ectopy. Potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. Which statement explains this?

options.A: Loop-induced hyperkalemia has blocked digoxin's effect
options.B: Furosemide has raised digoxin levels by blocking CYP3A4
options.C: Loop-induced hypokalemia has increased digoxin toxicity
options.D: Digoxin has caused the low potassium by wasting it
options.E: Furosemide ototoxicity is causing the visual symptoms

why: Loops cause hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. Hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity, so potassium, magnesium and creatinine are monitored.

whys.B: The taught link is through potassium, not CYP.
whys.D: The diuretic is the cause of the potassium loss.
whys.E: Ototoxicity affects hearing and follows rapid IV or high doses.

takeaway: Loop + digoxin: watch potassium.
discriminator: The diuretic sets up the toxicity; digoxin delivers it.

stem: A 52-year-old on clonidine three times daily runs out while travelling. Two days later blood pressure is 212/124 with headache and tremor. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Loss of thiazide effect because GFR fell below 30
options.B: Rebound hypertension from abrupt clonidine withdrawal
options.C: Nitrate tolerance from continuous dosing without a break
options.D: Reflex tachycardia and fluid retention from clonidine
options.E: Bradykinin accumulation after stopping the drug

why: Abrupt clonidine withdrawal causes rebound hypertension.

whys.A: No diuretic or renal change is described.
whys.C: He takes clonidine, not a nitrate.
whys.D: Those are hydralazine effects.
whys.E: Bradykinin belongs to ACE inhibitors.

takeaway: Never stop clonidine abruptly.
discriminator: Withdrawal effect vs adverse effect on the drug.

stem: A 58-year-old with diabetic kidney disease starts lisinopril. Two weeks later creatinine has risen from 1.4 to 1.7 mg/dL and potassium is 4.8 mEq/L. He feels well and is eating and drinking normally. What is the best action?

options.A: Continue lisinopril and recheck; a rise up to ~30% is expected
options.B: Switch to losartan, which does not change creatinine
options.C: Stop lisinopril; any creatinine rise means kidney injury
options.D: Add spironolactone to protect the kidney further
options.E: Add an NSAID to restore afferent arteriolar tone

why: An initial creatinine rise of up to about 30% reflects reduced intraglomerular pressure, not nephrotoxicity. Monitor potassium and renal function within 1–2 weeks; a larger rise warrants evaluation.

whys.B: ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole too.
whys.C: This is the classic trap: the rise is hemodynamic.
whys.D: That adds hyperkalemia risk and does not address this.
whys.E: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole and raise AKI risk.

takeaway: Up to ~30% creatinine rise on an ACE inhibitor: keep going.
discriminator: The benefit and the creatinine bump are the same action.

stem: A 66-year-old on eplerenone after a myocardial infarction starts a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. Which concern does the lecture attach to this combination?

options.A: Eplerenone causes more gynecomastia than spironolactone
options.B: Eplerenone induces CYP3A4 and clears the new drug
options.C: Eplerenone raises lithium levels as thiazides do
options.D: Eplerenone causes additive ototoxicity
options.E: Eplerenone interacts with CYP3A4 inhibitors; watch potassium

why: Eplerenone has fewer antiandrogen effects than spironolactone but interacts with CYP3A4 inhibitors; the class risk is hyperkalemia.

whys.B: The interaction taught is with inhibitors of CYP3A4.
whys.C: That is the thiazide interaction.
whys.D: That is loops with aminoglycosides.

takeaway: Eplerenone: CYP3A4 inhibitors matter.
discriminator: Fewer hormonal effects, but an added interaction.

stem: A 63-year-old with decompensated heart failure and pulmonary edema has a head injury with raised intracranial pressure. A resident suggests mannitol. What is the main concern?

options.A: Mannitol causes metabolic acidosis and potassium loss
options.B: Mannitol causes hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors
options.C: Mannitol causes gynecomastia through antiandrogen action
options.D: Mannitol loses efficacy once GFR is below about 30
options.E: Mannitol expands extracellular volume and can worsen overload

why: Mannitol is used for raised intracranial or intraocular pressure, but it expands extracellular volume: avoid it in heart failure and volume depletion. Monitor osmolality and electrolytes.

whys.B: That is the potassium-sparing class.
whys.C: That is spironolactone.
whys.D: That is the thiazide cutoff.

takeaway: Mannitol: right for ICP, wrong for a failing heart.
discriminator: It pulls water into the vessels before it leaves.

stem: A 46-year-old with hypertension has recurrent calcium kidney stones. A 68-year-old with hypertension has symptomatic hypercalcemia. Which pairing of diuretic to patient is correct?

options.A: A loop for both, since it is the most potent class
options.B: A loop for the stone former; thiazide for the hypercalcemia
options.C: Thiazide for the stone former; a loop for the hypercalcemia
options.D: Thiazide for both, since it lowers calcium everywhere
options.E: Acetazolamide for both, since it prevents kidney stones

why: Loops raise urinary calcium excretion; thiazides lower it. That makes a thiazide useful in calcium stones and a loop useful when serum calcium is high.

whys.B: Loops raise urinary calcium; thiazides raise serum calcium.
whys.D: It lowers urinary calcium but raises serum calcium.
whys.E: Acetazolamide is a cause of kidney stones.

takeaway: Loops lose calcium; thiazides keep it.
discriminator: Same electrolyte, opposite direction.

stem: A 69-year-old on lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days and is light-headed on standing. She asks what to do with her medicines. Which advice fits?

options.A: Continue everything; missed doses cause rebound hypertension
options.B: Add ibuprofen for the aches and keep all the others
options.C: Double the lisinopril to protect the kidney while ill
options.D: Hold the ACE inhibitor until she is eating and drinking again
options.E: Stop lisinopril permanently and never restart it

why: Sick-day rules: hold the ACE inhibitor or ARB during vomiting, diarrhea or dehydration, because RAAS blockade with reduced renal perfusion can precipitate AKI.

whys.B: That completes the triple whammy.
whys.C: RAAS blockade plus low perfusion can cause AKI.
whys.E: It is held during the illness, not abandoned.

takeaway: Vomiting or diarrhea: pause the ACE inhibitor or ARB.
discriminator: Temporary hold vs permanent stop.

stem: A 66-year-old on metoprolol after a myocardial infarction needs a calcium channel blocker for blood pressure. Which choice avoids a conduction problem, and what should she be told to expect?

options.A: Amlodipine; a slow pulse can occur
options.B: Amlodipine; ankle swelling can occur
options.C: Diltiazem; ankle swelling can occur
options.D: Verapamil; reflex tachycardia can occur
options.E: Verapamil; constipation can occur

why: Diltiazem or verapamil with a beta-blocker risks bradycardia and AV block; dihydropyridines pair with beta-blockers without that risk. Dihydropyridines cause peripheral edema and reflex tachycardia.

whys.A: Dihydropyridines cause reflex tachycardia, not bradycardia.
whys.C: Diltiazem with a beta-blocker carries the same conduction risk.
whys.D: Verapamil slows the heart.
whys.E: Verapamil with a beta-blocker risks bradycardia and AV block.

takeaway: With a beta-blocker, choose a dihydropyridine.
discriminator: Vessel-selective vs heart-slowing CCBs.

stem: A 70-year-old with CKD (GFR 24) has worsening leg edema and blood pressure 162/94 on hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, lisinopril and amlodipine. He takes all three reliably. Which change is most likely to help?

options.A: Replace hydrochlorothiazide with a loop diuretic
options.B: Stop lisinopril because the GFR is now under 30
options.C: Add hydralazine alone for its arteriolar dilation
options.D: Double the hydrochlorothiazide to 50 mg each day
options.E: Add clonidine as a fourth antihypertensive class

why: Thiazides lose efficacy below a GFR of about 30. In resistant hypertension with CKD, first confirm the diuretic is adequate; switching to a loop is often the most effective single change.

whys.B: Nothing here says the ACE inhibitor is the problem.
whys.C: It needs a beta-blocker and a diuretic, and does not fix volume.
whys.D: Thiazides fade below a GFR of about 30.
whys.E: The problem is an ineffective diuretic, not a missing class.

takeaway: GFR under ~30: thiazide out, loop in.
discriminator: A new class vs fixing the diuretic you already have.

stem: An 84-year-old with CKD is admitted with a serious infection and needs a renally cleared antibiotic. Her creatinine clearance is markedly reduced. Which dosing approach matches the lecture?

options.A: Reduced loading dose, then the usual maintenance dose
options.B: Avoid every renally cleared drug in any patient with CKD
options.C: Usual loading and usual maintenance, with levels if toxic
options.D: No loading dose, then double the interval and the dose
options.E: Usual loading dose, then a reduced maintenance dose

why: As GFR falls, renally cleared drugs accumulate. Check creatinine clearance, then lower the maintenance dose, extend the interval, or both. Loading doses are often unchanged.

whys.A: Loading is often unchanged; maintenance is what is adjusted.
whys.B: The drugs are adjusted, not banned.
whys.C: A renally cleared drug accumulates when GFR is low.
whys.D: Skipping the load delays effect; doubling the dose defeats the cut.

takeaway: Low GFR: keep the load, cut the maintenance.
discriminator: Loading fills the volume; maintenance replaces what is cleared.

stem: A 65-year-old with CKD has blood pressure above goal on an ACE inhibitor, amlodipine and an adequately dosed loop diuretic. Which add-on does the lecture name, and with what condition?

options.A: A thiazide in place of the loop, to add a new class
options.B: An NSAID, to reduce RAAS-driven volume retention
options.C: Spironolactone, with close potassium and renal monitoring
options.D: Verapamil added to the amlodipine for more CCB effect
options.E: Spironolactone, with no extra monitoring on an ACE inhibitor

why: Resistant hypertension is BP above goal despite three or more classes including a diuretic. Aldosterone antagonists can be added, with close potassium and renal-function monitoring, especially with an ACE inhibitor or ARB.

whys.B: NSAIDs blunt antihypertensives and raise AKI risk.
whys.D: This is not the taught add-on.
whys.E: The combination needs close potassium checks.

takeaway: Resistant hypertension: spironolactone, and watch potassium.
discriminator: The fourth drug shares a risk with the first.

stem: A 55-year-old man with resistant hypertension did well on spironolactone but has painful breast enlargement. Potassium is normal. Which change keeps the benefit and addresses the complaint?

options.A: Switch to eplerenone
options.B: Switch to acetazolamide for the same receptor effect
options.C: Continue spironolactone and add finasteride
options.D: Switch to triamterene and add trimethoprim
options.E: Switch to amiloride plus a potassium supplement

why: Spironolactone has antiandrogen effects (gynecomastia, menstrual irregularities) that eplerenone largely avoids. Both block the aldosterone receptor.

whys.B: It acts in the proximal tubule, not at the aldosterone receptor.
whys.C: That does not address the antiandrogen effect.
whys.D: Trimethoprim adds hyperkalemia risk.
whys.E: Supplements add hyperkalemia risk with potassium-sparing drugs.

takeaway: Gynecomastia on spironolactone: eplerenone.
discriminator: Same receptor, fewer antiandrogen effects.

stem: A 58-year-old with a documented severe sulfonamide allergy needs a diuretic. For which group does the lecture advise caution?

options.A: Only thiazides, never loops or acetazolamide
options.B: Only acetazolamide, never loops or thiazides
options.C: Spironolactone, eplerenone and amiloride
options.D: Loops, thiazides and acetazolamide
options.E: Mannitol, spironolactone and triamterene

why: Sulfonamide allergy: caution with loops, thiazides and acetazolamide.

whys.B: Loops and thiazides are included.
whys.C: These are not the sulfonamide-caution group.
whys.E: These are not the sulfonamide-caution group.

takeaway: Sulfa allergy: think loops, thiazides, acetazolamide.
discriminator: Three classes share the caution.

stem: A 76-year-old on losartan and spironolactone is treated for a urinary infection with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Five days later she is weak with peaked T waves. Which mechanism explains this?

options.A: Sulfamethoxazole displaced losartan and dropped her pressure
options.B: Trimethoprim added to two drugs that already raise potassium
options.C: Losartan caused bradykinin build-up and angioedema
options.D: The antibiotic caused hypokalemia through diarrhea
options.E: Trimethoprim induced the metabolism of spironolactone

why: Potassium supplements and trimethoprim cause hyperkalemia with potassium-sparing diuretics, and with ACE inhibitors and ARBs. Three potassium-raising drugs together is the setup.

whys.A: The finding is hyperkalemia, not hypotension.
whys.C: ARBs avoid the bradykinin effect, and this is not angioedema.
whys.D: Peaked T waves point to high potassium.
whys.E: Lower spironolactone effect would lower potassium.

takeaway: Trimethoprim counts as a potassium-raising drug.
discriminator: Count the potassium raisers before adding one.

stem: A 60-year-old with diabetes and two prior gout attacks starts hydrochlorothiazide. Which two problems is the drug most likely to worsen?

options.A: Hearing and magnesium, as with rapid IV dosing
options.B: Uric acid and urinary calcium, which both rise
options.C: Serum potassium and gynecomastia
options.D: Blood glucose and uric acid
options.E: Blood glucose and serum potassium, which both rise

why: Thiazides cause hyperglycemia and hyperuricemia (can precipitate gout), along with hyponatremia, hypokalemia and hypercalcemia.

whys.B: Thiazides lower urinary calcium.
whys.C: Those are spironolactone concerns.
whys.E: Potassium falls on a thiazide.

takeaway: Thiazide in a diabetic with gout: watch glucose and uric acid.
discriminator: Thiazide highs vs thiazide lows.

stem: A 57-year-old with resistant hypertension is started on hydralazine alone. A week later he has a racing pulse and swollen ankles. What was omitted?

options.A: A slow taper to prevent rebound
options.B: A potassium check within 1 week
options.C: A nitrate-free interval each night
options.D: A switch to an ARB for the cough
options.E: A beta-blocker and a diuretic alongside it

why: Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and fluid retention, so it must be paired with a beta-blocker and a diuretic.

whys.B: That is spironolactone monitoring.
whys.C: That is for long-acting nitrates.
whys.D: That is the ACE-inhibitor cough.

takeaway: Hydralazine never travels alone.
discriminator: The partners treat its two reflex effects.

stem: A 77-year-old stable on digoxin starts verapamil for rate control. Ten days later she has nausea, anorexia and a pulse of 44. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.A: Verapamil raised her digoxin level
options.B: Rifampin-like induction cleared the verapamil
options.C: Verapamil caused hypokalemia like a loop diuretic
options.D: Grapefruit juice raised her verapamil level
options.E: Verapamil lowered her digoxin level

why: Verapamil and diltiazem raise digoxin levels; both drugs also slow the heart.

whys.B: Induction lowers CCB levels and would not slow the pulse.
whys.C: Verapamil does not waste potassium.
whys.D: Grapefruit raises dihydropyridine levels; none is mentioned.
whys.E: A lower level would not cause toxicity.

takeaway: Verapamil or diltiazem + digoxin: expect a higher digoxin level.
discriminator: Loops harm through potassium; verapamil through the level.

stem: A 71-year-old with heart failure was well controlled on furosemide. After 10 days of naproxen for back pain he has gained 4 kg and creatinine has risen. Which explanation fits?

options.A: The NSAID blunted the diuretic and raised AKI risk
options.B: Furosemide tolerance needs a diuretic-free interval
options.C: The NSAID raised furosemide levels and caused toxicity
options.D: The NSAID caused hypokalemia that blocked the loop
options.E: The NSAID dilated the efferent arteriole

why: NSAIDs blunt the diuretic effect and raise AKI risk.

whys.B: Drug-free intervals are for nitrates.
whys.C: More loop effect would cause weight loss.
whys.D: This is not the taught mechanism.
whys.E: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole.

takeaway: NSAID + diuretic: less diuresis, more kidney risk.
discriminator: Loss of effect and harm from the same added drug.
